    "## Mission Briefing\n",
    "\n",

    "\n",
    "The City Council has commissioned the \"Future City\" initiative. Before we can build advanced Artificial Intelligence agents, we must first build the basic digital infrastructure to process data.\n",
    "\n",
    "Your task is to write the code for the **TrafficGuard Legacy System**. This system will manually process vehicle data from roadside sensors using explicit logic (rules). This infrastructure will serve as the foundation for the AI systems we will build in Phase II.\n"

    "## Learning Objectives\n",
    "\n",
    "By completing this assignment, you will master:\n",
    "\n",
    "- **The Environment:** Navigating Jupyter Notebooks (Cells, Markdown, Execution).\n",
    "- **Data Representation:** Using Variables (Strings, Integers, Floats).\n",
    "- **Logic Control:** Writing explicit rules using `if`, `elif`, and `else`.\n",
    "- **Data Structures:** Managing traffic queues using Lists and Dictionaries.\n",
    "- **Automation:** Creating Functions and Loops to process data streams.\n",
    "- **Data Viz:** \"Seeing\" the data before coding.\n",
    "- **Linear Regression:** Predicting values with a simple line.\n",
    "- **The Neuron:** Understanding the math of classification ($w \\cdot x + b$).\n",
    "- **AI Safety:** Building guardrails for when the AI hallucinates.\n",
    "\n",
    "**Submission format:** Completed Jupyter Notebook (`.ipynb`)  \n",
    "**Suggested file name:** `TrafficGuard_YourName.ipynb`\n"

    "Create an infinite loop (code provided below) and practice using the \"Interrupt Kernel\" (Stop Button) to regain control.\n"

     "text": [
      "Starting safety drill...\n",
      "System running... 0\n",

     ]

   ],
   "source": [
    "import time\n",
    "\n",
    "max_steps = 5  # Optional drill: increase this number, run the cell, then interrupt it.\n",
    "print(\"Starting safety drill...\")\n",
    "\n",
    "counter = 0\n",
    "while counter < max_steps:\n",
    "    print(f\"System running... {counter}\")\n",
    "    counter += 1\n",
    "    time.sleep(1)\n",
    "\n",
    "print(\"Safety drill finished.\")\n"
   ]

    "## Part 4: Automation (Functions & Loops)\n",
    "\n",
    "**Objective:** Processing data at scale.\n",
    "\n",
    "We cannot write `if/else` statements manually for every car. We need a \"Function\"--a reusable machine.\n",
    "\n",
    "1. Define a function named `calculate_toll(length, is_emergency)`.\n",
    "2. Move your logic from Part 2 inside this function so it returns the price.\n",
    "3. **Batch Processing:** Write a `for` loop that goes through your `traffic_queue` list. Inside the loop, call your function for every length and print the toll.\n"
   ]
  },
  {
   "cell_type": "code",
   "execution_count": 32,
   "id": "e990e34a",
   "metadata": {
    "executionInfo": {
     "elapsed": 38,
     "status": "ok",
     "timestamp": 1783690458245,
     "user": {
      "displayName": "Shreyash Chandak",
      "userId": "00100992251653739073"
     },
     "user_tz": -330
    },
    "id": "e990e34a"
   },
   "outputs": [],
   "source": [
    "# TODO: Complete the function.\n",
    "# It should return 0 for emergency vehicles, 50 for heavy vehicles, and 10 for light vehicles.\n",
    "\n",
    "def calculate_toll(length, is_emergency=False):\n",
    "    # Write your logic here.\n",
    "    toll = 0\n",
    "    if is_emergency:\n",
    "        print(\"Class: Emergency Vehicle. Toll: $0\")\n",
    "        toll = 0\n",
    "    elif length > 10:\n",
    "        print(\"Class: Heavy Vehicle. Toll: $50\")\n",
    "        toll = 50\n",
    "    else:\n",
    "        print(\"Class: Light Vehicle. Toll: $10\")\n",
    "        toll = 10\n",
    "    return toll"
   ]
  },

    "# TODO: Process every vehicle in traffic_queue using a for loop.\n",
    "\n",
    "total_revenue = 0\n",
    "print(\"--- Starting Batch Processing ---\")\n",

    "# Example structure:\n",
    "for car_length in traffic_queue:\n",
    "    price = calculate_toll(car_length)\n",

    "    total_revenue += price\n",
    "\n",

    "# Generate 50 cars: short length, light weight.\n",
    "cars_length = np.random.uniform(3, 5, 50)\n",
    "cars_weight = np.random.uniform(1, 2, 50)\n",
    "\n",
    "# Generate 50 trucks: long length, heavy weight.\n",
    "trucks_length = np.random.uniform(10, 15, 50)\n",
    "trucks_weight = np.random.uniform(5, 10, 50)\n",
    "\n",
    "# Combine features and labels.\n",
    "X_cars = np.column_stack((cars_length, cars_weight))\n",
    "y_cars = np.zeros(50)   # 0 = Light vehicle / car\n",
    "\n",
    "X_trucks = np.column_stack((trucks_length, trucks_weight))\n",
    "y_trucks = np.ones(50)  # 1 = Heavy vehicle / truck\n",
    "\n",
    "X = np.vstack((X_cars, X_trucks))\n",
    "y = np.hstack((y_cars, y_trucks))\n",
    "\n",
    "print(X)\n",
    "print(f\"Dataset generated. Total vehicles: {len(X)}\")\n"
   ]

    "### Exploratory Analysis Questions\n",
    "\n",
    "Look at the plot and answer:\n",
    "\n",
    "1. Is there a clean empty space between the car cluster and the truck cluster?\n",
    "2. Imagine a billboard with `length = 15` and `weight = 0.2`. Where would it appear on this graph?\n",
    "3. Does it sit inside the truck cluster? Why or why not?\n",
    "\n",
    "**Answer:**  \n",
    "(Double click here to write your answer.)\n",
    "\n",
    "1. Yes, there is mostly a clear empty space between the car cluster and the truck cluster.  \n",
    "   The car points are grouped around shorter length and lower weight, while the truck points are grouped around longer length and higher weight.\n",
    "\n",
    "2. A billboard with `length = 15` and `weight = 0.2` would appear far to the right on the graph because of its large length, but very low near the bottom because of its extremely small weight.\n",
    "\n",
    "3. No, it does not sit inside the truck cluster.  \n",
    "   Even though its length is similar to a truck, its weight is much smaller than the truck points.  \n",
    "   So it becomes an outlier. This shows why using only one feature like length can give the wrong classification, and why using both length and weight is better.\n"
   ]

    "## Part 7: The Line of Best Fit (Manual Regression)\n",
    "\n",
    "**Objective:** Intuition for \"Weights\" and \"Bias\" using simple pricing.\n",
    "\n",
    "Before we classify types, let's try to predict the toll price based on weight.\n",
    "\n",
    "$$\\text{Price} = (m \\times \\text{Weight}) + c$$\n",
    "\n",
    "1. We assume the relationship is linear: `Price = (m * Weight) + c`.\n",
    "2. **Visualize & Minimize:** Run the helper function `visualize_regressor(m, c)`.\n",
    "3. **Manual Tuning:** Start with `m = 0`, `c = 0`. Note the high error score. Adjust `m` (slope) and `c` (intercept) until the line passes through the data and the Error Metric is minimized (closest to 0).\n",
    "4. **Concept Check:** What does `m` represent in the real world? (Hint: Cost per ton).\n"
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "def visualize_regressor(m, c):\n",
    "    \"\"\"Visualize y = mx + c against a simple pricing dataset.\"\"\"\n",
    "    weights = np.array([1, 2, 5, 8, 10])\n",
    "    actual_prices = np.array([15, 25, 55, 85, 105])\n",
    "\n",
    "    predicted_prices = (m * weights) + c\n",
    "    avg_error = np.mean(np.abs(actual_prices - predicted_prices))\n",
    "\n",
    "    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))\n",
    "    plt.scatter(weights, actual_prices, color=\"green\", s=100, label=\"Actual Data\")\n",
    "    plt.plot(weights, predicted_prices, color=\"purple\", linewidth=3, label=\"Your Line\")\n",
    "\n",
    "    plt.xlabel(\"Weight (tons)\")\n",
    "    plt.ylabel(\"Toll Price ($)\")\n",
    "    plt.title(f\"Linear Regression Tuning | Average Error: ${avg_error:.2f}\")\n",
    "    plt.legend()\n",
    "    plt.grid(True)\n",
    "    plt.show()\n",
    "\n",
    "    print(f\"Average Error: ${avg_error:.2f}\")\n"
   ]

    "## Part 8: The Manual Neuron (The MCP Model)\n",
    "\n",
    "**Objective:** Implementing the math of a single neuron.\n",
    "\n",
    "Now, let's switch to classification (Heavy vs Light). A neuron is just a line that separates two groups.\n",
    "\n",
    "$$z = (w_1 \\times \\text{length}) + (w_2 \\times \\text{weight}) + b$$\n",
    "\n",
    "1. **Implement the Neuron Formula** as a Python function.\n",
    "2. **The Activation:** If `z > 0`, return `1` (Heavy). If `z <= 0`, return `0` (Light).\n",
    "3. **Interactive Tuning:** Use the provided function `visualize_decision_boundary(w1, w2, bias)`.\n",
    "4. **Task:** Manually change the weights until the Decision Boundary (the line) perfectly separates the Red dots from the Blue dots.\n"
   ]
  },

   "source": [
    "# TODO: Implement the neuron formula.\n",
    "\n",
    "def manual_neuron(length, weight, w1, w2, bias):\n",
    "    # Write your logic here.\n",
    "    z = (w1 * length) + (w2 * weight) + bias\n",
    "    \n",
    "    if z > 0:\n",
    "        return 1\n",
    "    else:\n",
    "        return 0\n"
   ]

    "def visualize_decision_boundary(w1, w2, bias):\n",
    "    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))\n",
    "    plt.scatter(X_cars[:, 0], X_cars[:, 1], color=\"blue\", label=\"Cars / Light\")\n",
    "    plt.scatter(X_trucks[:, 0], X_trucks[:, 1], color=\"red\", label=\"Trucks / Heavy\")\n",
    "\n",
    "    x_vals = np.linspace(0, 16, 100)\n",
    "    if w2 != 0:\n",
    "        y_vals = -(w1 * x_vals + bias) / w2\n",
    "        plt.plot(x_vals, y_vals, color=\"black\", linewidth=2, linestyle=\"--\", label=\"Decision Boundary\")\n",
    "    else:\n",
    "        print(\"w2 is 0, so the boundary cannot be drawn as y = mx + c.\")\n",
    "\n",
    "    plt.xlim(0, 18)\n",
    "    plt.ylim(0, 12)\n",
    "    plt.xlabel(\"Length (m)\")\n",
    "    plt.ylabel(\"Weight (tons)\")\n",
    "    plt.title(f\"Manual Neuron: {w1}*L + {w2}*W + {bias} = 0\")\n",
    "    plt.legend()\n",
    "    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)\n",
    "    plt.show()\n"
   ]

    "## Part 9: Automated Learning (Scikit-Learn)\n",
    "\n",
    "**Objective:** Letting the machine find the weights.\n",
    "\n",
    "Hand-tuning is tedious. We will use `scikit-learn` to calculate the optimal `w` and `b` instantly.\n",
    "\n",
    "\n",

    "def traffic_system_verified(length, weight):\n",
    "    # --- LAYER 1: Safety Guardrails ---\n",
    "    if weight < 0:\n",
    "        return \"ERROR: ANOMALY DETECTED - Negative weight is impossible\"\n",
    "    if length <= 0:\n",
    "        return \"ERROR: ANOMALY DETECTED - Invalid vehicle length\"\n",
    "    if weight > 100:\n",
    "        return \"ERROR: ANOMALY DETECTED - Weight exceeds physical maximum\"\n",
    "\n",
    "    # Example: if weight < 0, return \"ERROR: ANOMALY DETECTED\".\n",
    "\n",
    "    # <YOUR CODE HERE>\n",
    "\n",
    "    # --- LAYER 2: AI Model ---\n",
    "    features = [[length, weight]]\n",
    "    prediction = model.predict(features)\n",
    "\n",
    "    if prediction[0] == 1:\n",
    "        return \"Heavy Vehicle\"\n",
    "    else:\n",
    "        return \"Light Vehicle\"\n",
    "\n",
    "# --- TEST YOUR SYSTEM ---\n",
    "print(\"Test 1 (Ghost Vehicle):\", traffic_system_verified(4, -50))\n",
    "print(\"Test 2 (Delivery Van):  \", traffic_system_verified(6, 3.5))\n"

    "**The AI Engineer's Dilemma:**\n",

    "\"In Part 8, you manually found the weights. In Part 9, the computer found them. In Part 10, you had to write manual `if` statements again.\"\n",
    "\n",
    "**Question:** If AI is so smart, why do we still need manual guardrails (Part 10)? Why can't we trust the math 100%?\n",

    "**Answer:**\n",
    "AI is smart, but it only knows patterns from training data. It has no understanding of the real world. When I fed the ghost vehicle (weight = -50) to the model, it still gave a prediction because the math doesn't know that negative weight is impossible. The model just does multiplication and comparison. It has no concept of \"this makes no sense\".\n",
    "That's why we still need manual guardrails. The if weight < 0 check is something a human engineer adds based on domain knowledge, something the model can never learn from data alone. AI finds patterns, engineers add safety. Both are needed together to build a reliable system.\n"
